summary: This informational memo describes the framework of the Next Steps in Signaling working group for protocols that signal information about a data flow along its path through the network. The NSIS suite is meant to support applications that install or change state in network nodes.

plainLanguage.summary: Next Steps in Signaling (NSIS) is a framework for messages that help network nodes manage state related to a data flow. It separates moving the messages from interpreting what each signaling application asks the network to do.

subtitle: A framework for signaling about data flows using a generic transport layer and application-specific protocols.

tldr.problem: Network signaling needs to install, change, or read state related to data flows, and the same mechanisms should support more than quality-of-service reservations.
tldr.mechanism: NSIS separates hop-by-hop message transport (NTLP) from application-specific signaling protocols (NSLPs). The framework discusses path coupling, identifiers, routing changes, mobility, and example applications.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes an architecture and requirements, not detailed protocol designs. Its initial focus is path-coupled signaling for unicast flows.

today: RFC 4080 is Informational. The work-unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the memo describes a framework rather than detailed protocol designs.

sections.title: The Signaling Problem
sections.content:
NSIS considers protocols that carry information about a data flow along its path through a network. The path is already determined by routing; this framework does not signal to create routes. The initial problem is limited to unicast flows and path-coupled signaling, where messages follow the data path through participating nodes.

The framework generalizes earlier signaling work in two ways: it should work without a complete end-to-end deployment, and it should support purposes beyond quality of service. The initial applications discussed are quality-of-service and middlebox signaling.
sections.plainLanguage: Network nodes sometimes need messages about a particular flow, such as a request to reserve resources. NSIS sets out a common framework for sending those messages and supporting different uses.

sections.title: Flows, Sessions, and Signaling Paths
sections.content:
An NSIS Entity (NE) is the function in a node that implements an NSIS protocol. Only some nodes on a data path need an NE. Two NEs that communicate directly are peers; this relationship does not necessarily correspond to one IP hop.

A flow is a unidirectional sequence of packets that follows a path and can be distinguished by a classifier. A session is an application-level exchange for which network state is managed or monitored. A session may map to more than one flow, which allows signaling to relate a flow change to the same wider exchange.

Path-coupled signaling passes through NEs on the data path. Path-decoupled signaling can reach nodes away from that path. The initial NSIS work focuses mainly on path-coupled operation, though the framework also describes hosts, network edges, and proxies as possible signaling endpoints.
sections.plainLanguage: A flow is one stream of packets along a route. A session can connect several flows to the same application exchange, even if the route changes.

sections.title: The Two Protocol Layers
sections.content:
The NSIS suite has a generic transport layer called the NSIS Transport Layer Protocol (NTLP), plus signaling application protocols called NSIS Signaling Layer Protocols (NSLPs). The NTLP moves messages between adjacent NEs. An NSLP defines the messages and behavior for an application such as quality-of-service signaling.

At an intermediate node, the NTLP can pass a message along when no local NSLP needs to process it. The layers manage different kinds of state: the NTLP provides message delivery, while the NSLP handles the meaning and lifetime of application state. The framework leaves detailed NTLP design open.
sections.plainLanguage: One layer carries a signaling message to the next participating node. A separate layer understands what the message means for its particular job.

sections.title: Transport Functions and Network Changes
sections.content:
The NTLP may need to locate peers, deliver messages in either direction, support optional reliability, handle large messages, and avoid creating congestion. The framework discusses two addressing styles: a message can name the next peer, or it can be sent toward the data destination and intercepted along the way. Both have uses.

Signaling must interact with routing changes, mobility, multihoming, NATs, and tunnels. When a route changes, state may need to be installed along the new path and removed from the old one. A session identifier can help relate changed flows to the same session. The memo describes these as architectural considerations rather than prescribing one universal solution.
sections.plainLanguage: The message layer must account for ordinary network changes, including new routes and changed addresses. The application layer decides how to update the state that its messages manage.

sections.title: Quality of Service and Other Applications
sections.content:
The memo gives quality-of-service signaling as a detailed example. A requesting entity asks for network resources, intermediate entities forward the signaling, a responding entity can accept or reject it, and a resource-management function decides what resources are available. Example operations include requesting, modifying, releasing, accepting, rejecting, notifying, and refreshing state.

Other possible uses include installing flow-related state in firewalls or NATs, network monitoring, testing, and tunnel endpoint discovery. These examples illustrate the framework; they do not establish an overarching Internet resource-management architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: One application can ask for network resources and receive an answer. The same layered framework could support other tasks, such as managing a firewall or gathering information about a flow.
